claim: Microtubules have an approximate inner diameter of 15 nm and outer diameter of 25 nm.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are long slender hollow cylindrical filaments with an approximate inner and outer diameter of 15 nm and 25 nm (Nogales et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nogales et al., 1999

claim: Microtubules are an indispensable structural element in biology.
source: They are an indispensable structural element in biology, and their mechanical properties play an critical role in defining the shape and functionalities of various cellular architectures including neuronal axons, cilia and flagella, centrioles as well as the mitotic spindle (Howard, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howard, 2001

claim: Microtubule mechanical properties play a critical role in defining the shape and functionalities of various cellular architectures including neuronal axons, cilia and flagella, centrioles and the mitotic spindle.
source: They are an indispensable structural element in biology, and their mechanical properties play an critical role in defining the shape and functionalities of various cellular architectures including neuronal axons, cilia and flagella, centrioles as well as the mitotic spindle (Howard, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howard, 2001

claim: There is considerable disagreement between different reported values of microtubule elastic moduli.
source: However, there is a considerable disagreement between different reported values of MT elastic moduli (Mickey and Howard, 1995), the dependence of the elastic moduli on the presence of stabilizing agents (taxol and GMPCPP), as well as a possible length-dependence of flexural rigidity (Pampaloni et al., 2006; Kis et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mickey and Howard, 1995; Pampaloni et al., 2006; Kis et al., 2002

claim: Thermal fluctuation measurements of microtubules only induce small strain deformations.
source: Because of significant rigidity of MTs these two types of measurements typically probe different deformation (strain) regimes. Thermally induced fluctuations only induce small strain deformations, while methods that use external forces are more suited to probe the high-strain regime.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the significant rigidity of microtubules

claim: External force methods are more suited to probe the high-strain regime of microtubules.
source: Because of significant rigidity of MTs these two types of measurements typically probe different deformation (strain) regimes. Thermally induced fluctuations only induce small strain deformations, while methods that use external forces are more suited to probe the high-strain regime.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the significant rigidity of microtubules

claim: The majority of measurements that rely on filament fluctuations in the low strain regime yield values of microtubule flexural rigidity around a certain value.
source: Careful review of this data shows that the majority of measurements that rely on the filament fluctuations in the low strain regime yield values of microtubule flexural rigidity around , while measurements at high strains, tend to be for similarly prepared MTs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Supplementary file 2

claim: Measurements at high strains tend to yield lower flexural rigidity values for similarly prepared microtubules compared to low strain measurements.
source: Careful review of this data shows that the majority of measurements that rely on the filament fluctuations in the low strain regime yield values of microtubule flexural rigidity around , while measurements at high strains, tend to be for similarly prepared MTs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Supplementary file 2

claim: Above a critical strain, microtubules deviate from the classical Euler-Bernoulli elastic filament model, showing a softening response with increasing deformations.
source: We find that, while in the low-strain regime, microtubules may be quantitatively described in terms of the classical Euler-Bernoulli elastic filament, above a critical strain they deviate from this simple elastic model, showing a softening response with increasingdeformations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optical trapping measurements

claim: A three-dimensional thin-shell model captures the softening effect of microtubules in the high strain regime.
source: A three-dimensional thin-shell model, in which the increased mechanical compliance is caused by flattening and eventual buckling of the filament cross-section, captures this softening effect in the high strain regime and yields quantitative values of the effective mechanical properties of microtubules.
evidence: Supported by simulation results that match experimental data

claim: The increased mechanical compliance of microtubules at high strain is caused by flattening and eventual buckling of the filament cross-section.
source: A three-dimensional thin-shell model, in which the increased mechanical compliance is caused by flattening and eventual buckling of the filament cross-section, captures this softening effect in the high strain regime and yields quantitative values of the effective mechanical properties of microtubules.
evidence: Supported by simulation results showing cross-sectional deformation

claim: Microtubule properties are highly dependent on the magnitude of the applied strain.
source: Our results demonstrate that properties of microtubules are highly dependent on the magnitude of the applied strain and offer a new interpretation for the large variety in microtubule mechanical data measured by different methods.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing different behavior at different strain regimes

claim: Bacterial flagellar filaments have a hollow core with a diameter of only 2 nm.
source: Furthermore, like microtubules flagella have a hollow core; however, their core diameter is only 2 nm.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the manuscript

claim: Flagella should effectively behave as solid cylinders due to their small hollow core.
source: Furthermore, like microtubules flagella have a hollow core; however, their core diameter is only 2 nm. Therefore flagella should effectively behave as solid cylinders.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the small core diameter

claim: Flagellin monomers from Salmonella typhimurium strain SJW1660 have a point mutation that causes them to assemble into straight filaments.
source: We use flagellin monomers isolated from Salmonella typhimurium, strain SJW1660, which have a point mutation in their amino-acid sequence that causes them to assemble into straight filaments (Kamiya et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamiya et al., 1980

claim: A simple Euler-Bernoulli beam model quantitatively describes the measured force curve of flagellar filaments in all strain regimes.
source: A simple model based on Euler-Bernoullibeams quantitatively describes the measured force curve in all strain regimes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and simulation results for flagella

claim: The buckling force of microtubules increases linearly in the initial low strain region.
source: In the compression region, which corresponds to microtubule bending, the buckling force increases linearly in the initial (low strain) region, but quickly deviates from this trend and saturates at some critical strain, and it gradually decreases at high strain values.
evidence: Supported by experimental force-strain measurements

claim: The buckling force of microtubules saturates at some critical strain.
source: In the compression region, which corresponds to microtubule bending, the buckling force increases linearly in the initial (low strain) region, but quickly deviates from this trend and saturates at some critical strain, and it gradually decreases at high strain values.
evidence: Supported by experimental force-strain measurements

claim: The buckling force of microtubules gradually decreases at high strain values.
source: In the compression region, which corresponds to microtubule bending, the buckling force increases linearly in the initial (low strain) region, but quickly deviates from this trend and saturates at some critical strain, and it gradually decreases at high strain values.
evidence: Supported by experimental force-strain measurements

claim: The softening behavior of microtubules cannot be captured by the ideal Euler-Bernoulli model.
source: Such behavior indicates softening of MTs, an outcome that cannot be captured by the ideal Euler-Bernoulli model.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data with 1D model predictions

claim: The mechanical response of microtubules is well-captured by an anisotropic elastic shell model with three coarse grained elastic parameters (one shear, and two stretching moduli).
source: We show that the mechanical response of MTs is well-captured by an anisotropic elastic shell model with three coarse grained elastic parameters (oneshear, and two stretching moduli).
evidence: Supported by simulation results that match experimental data

claim: Cross-sectional flattening and buckling in response to compressive radial strains has been described for microtubule filaments.
source: For microtubule filaments in particular, cross-sectional flattening and buckling in response to compressive radial strains has also been described (Kononova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kononova et al., 2014

claim: The force-strain curve of flagellar filaments is qualitatively different from that observed for microtubules.
source: The measured strain-force curve of a flagellar filament is qualitatively different from that observed for microtubules (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In both the compression and extension regime, the force on flagellar filaments monotonically increases.
source: In both the compression and extension regime, the force monotonically increases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data for flagella

claim: The slope in the extension region is higher than that in the compression region for flagellar filaments.
source: We also note that the slope in the extension region is higher than that in the compression region.
evidence: Supported by experimental data for flagella

claim: In response to extensional forces, the flagellar filament bends in the proximity of the bead attachment point.
source: Because the force is not applied along the filament centerline, in response to extensional forces the filament bends in the proximity of the bead attachments point.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the experimental setup geometry

claim: The one-dimensional model is not capable of reproducing the complex elastic behavior observed in microtubule filaments.
source: However, the same one-dimensional model is not capable of reproducing the more complex elastic behavior observed in microtubule filaments.
evidence: Supported by comparison of 1D model predictions with experimental data

claim: The 1D model can at most describe the low strain regime of the microtubule force-compression curve.
source: At most, it can describe the low strain regime of the force-compression curve (Figure 2B, green dashed curve).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2B

claim: The 3D model of microtubules explicitly accounts for their hollow center.
source: To explain theelastic behavior of microtubules over the entire strain regime we developed a more comprehensive 3D model of microtubules that explicitly accounts for their hollow center.
evidence: Description of the model construction

claim: The 3D microtubule model quantitatively explains the softening observed in experimentally measured force-strain curves.
source: The 3D microtubule model quantitatively explains the softening that is observed in experimentally measured force-strain curves of microtubules.
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data

claim: Microtubules are highly anisotropic materials.
source: This observation confirms that microtubules are highly anisotropic materials.
evidence: Inferred from the large difference between Ea and Ec values

claim: The large shear modulus values likely indicate that microtubule deformations in the experiments are large enough to reach the point of deforming the tubulin units themselves rather than the bonds between them.
source: This likely indicates that the microtubule deformations in our experiments are large enough to reach the point of deforming the tubulin units themselves rather than the bonds between them (see Discussion).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the high shear modulus values

claim: The decrease in the buckling force is directly associated with ovalisation of the microtubule cross-section.
source: The decrease in the buckling force is directly associated with ovalisation of the microtubulecross-section.
evidence: Supported by simulation results showing cross-sectional deformation

claim: Cross-sectional deformations vanish at the endpoints (at the locations of the optical beads).
source: While cross-sectional deformations vanish at the endpoints (i.e. at the locations of the optical beads, shown in blue), deformations in the interior are considerable.
evidence: Supported by simulation results

claim: Deformations in the interior of the microtubule are considerable.
source: While cross-sectional deformations vanish at the endpoints (i.e. at the locations of the optical beads, shown in blue), deformations in the interior are considerable.
evidence: Supported by simulation results

claim: The cross-section is circular until a critical bending moment is reached.
source: This is indeed what we observe - the cross-section is circular (Figure 5B, green and blue curves) until a critical bending moment is reached.
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5B

claim: With further compression, subsequent kinks can develop one at a time in the vicinity of the first kink.
source: With further compression, subsequent kinks can develop - one at a time - in its vicinity.
evidence: Supported by simulation results

claim: Discontinuities in the curvature profile of a filament signal the existence of cross-sectional ovalization and eventual kinking.
source: Thus, discontinuities in the curvature profile of a filament signal the existence of cross-sectional ovalization and eventual kinking.
evidence: Inferred from the correspondence between curvature and flatness profiles

claim: The formation of kinks can be identified directly from the force-strain plots as a small drop in the buckling force.
source: In simulations, the formation of kinks can be identified directly from the force-strain plots as a small drop in the buckling force (Figure 5A, red).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5A

claim: Hysteresis associated with forward and backward compression is observed in simulations in which the filament forms kinks.
source: Indeed, hysteresis associated with forward and backward compressionis observed in simulations in which the filament forms kinks.
evidence: Supported by simulation results

claim: Critical curvatures for microtubule softening are likely reached and exceeded in the beating flagella of Chlamydomonas.
source: Such values are small enough that they are likely reached and exceeded at least in some systems both in vivo, as in the beating flagella of Chlamydomonas (Sartori et al., 2016; Geyer et al., 2016) and in vitro, as in microtubule rings observed in gliding assays (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sartori et al., 2016; Geyer et al., 2016

claim: Critical curvatures for microtubule softening are likely reached and exceeded in microtubule rings observed in gliding assays.
source: Such values are small enough that they are likely reached and exceeded at least in some systems both in vivo, as in the beating flagella of Chlamydomonas (Sartori et al., 2016; Geyer et al., 2016) and in vitro, as in microtubule rings observed in gliding assays (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011

claim: Microtubule softening is a consequence of cross-sectional deformations enabled by a small circumferential Young's modulus of a few MPa.
source: The simulations reveal that microtubule softening is a consequence of cross-sectional deformations enabled by a small circumferential Young's modulus of a few MPa.
evidence: Supported by simulation results and fitting to experimental data

claim: Lateral bonds between adjacent protofilaments are much weaker than longitudinal bonds along protofilaments.
source: While it is known that MTs do not behave as isotropic Euler-Bernoulli slender rods - since, for instance, lateral bonds between adjacent protofilaments are much weaker than longitudinal bonds along protofilaments (Nogales et al., 1999; VanBuren et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Nogales et al., 1999; VanBuren et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2008

claim: Many groups have used the Euler-Bernoulli beam model to interpret their microtubule data.
source: many groups have used the Euler-Bernoulli beam model to interpret their data (Kikumoto et al., 2006; Brangwynne et al., 2006; Li, 2008; Takasone et al., 2002; Jiang and Zhang, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The Timoshenko beam model remains inadequate for microtubules since it does not allow for anisotropy between the axial and circumferential directions.
source: This model remains inadequate, however, since it does not allow for anisotropy between the axial and circumferential directions, which is substantial and plays an important role in the mechanical behavior of MTs (Deriu et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2008; Tuszyński et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deriu et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2008; Tuszyński et al., 2005

claim: The average flexural rigidity of Taxol stabilized microtubules found via thermal fluctuations is more than twice as large as the average rigidity found from force-based experiments.
source: Indeed, a comprehensive summary of experimental results on MT flexural rigidity (Hawkins et al., 2010) strongly supports this interpretation: for example, the average flexural rigidity of Taxol stabilized MTs found via thermal fluctuations is more than twice as large as the average rigidity found from force-based experiments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hawkins et al., 2010

claim: Small radial deformations only impact the weak bridges between adjacent protofilaments, while larger ones may deform the tubulin dimers.
source: The discrepancy can be reconciled by noting that small radial deformations only impactthe weak bridges between adjacent protofilaments, while larger ones may deform the tubulin dimers, which, like typical proteins, have a high stiffness in the GPa range (Huang et al., 2008; Pampaloni et al., 2006; Needleman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2008; Pampaloni et al., 2006; Needleman et al., 2005

claim: Inter-protofilament bonds may be very compliant for small deformations (on the 0.2 nm scale), while larger deviations may approach the limit of physically deforming the tubulin units.
source: However, inter-protofilament bonds may be very compliant for small deformations (on the 0.2 nm scale), while larger deviations may approach the limit of physically deforming the tubulin units (Pampaloni et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pampaloni et al., 2006

claim: A strain on the order of −0.01 would lead to deformations on the 0.2 nm scale.
source: Following estimates in (Pampaloni et al., 2006), a strain on the order of −0.01 would lead to deformations on the 0.2 nm scale, while our experiments routinely go up to much larger strains around −0.2.
evidence: Based on estimates from Pampaloni et al., 2006 and experimental strain values

claim: The large values obtained for shear modulus are likely due to large shear deformations that surpass the elastic limits of inter-protofilament bonds.
source: Therefore, it's likely that the large values we obtained for shear modulus are due to large shear deformations that surpass the elastic limits of inter-protofilament bonds.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the magnitude of experimental strains

claim: Sufficiently large deformations can induce reversible breaking of lateral contacts between protofilaments and eventually even of longitudinal contacts between subunits in a protofilament.
source: Notably, sufficiently large deformations can induce (reversible) breaking of lateral contacts between protofilaments and eventually even of longitudinal contacts between subunits in a protofilament as observed in radial indentation simulations (Kononova et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017) and corroborated with scanning force microscopy experiments (Schaap et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kononova et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Schaap et al., 2004

claim: Contact breaking may constitute an alternate or co-occurring reason for the large shear modulus obtained from fitting experimental data.
source: Therefore, contact breaking may constitute an alternate or co-occurring reason for the large shear modulus obtained from fitting our experimental data.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on literature about contact breaking

claim: Microtubule softening may decrease microtubule susceptibility to mechanical failure or depolymerization.
source: We may thus speculate about the biological significance of MT softening, with one hypothesis being that it decreases MT susceptibility to mechanical failure or depolymerization (Mohrbach et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis with citation to Mohrbach et al., 2012

claim: Repeated large-scale deformations locally damage dynamical microtubules, which leads to effectively softer filaments.
source: In particular, this study demonstrated that repeated large-scale deformations locally damage microtubules, which leads to effectively softer filaments.
evidence: Referring to findings from Schaedel et al., 2015

claim: Damage to dynamical microtubules is accompanied by a loss of tubulin monomers.
source: This damageis accompanied by a loss of tubulin monomers.
evidence: Referring to findings from Schaedel et al., 2015

claim: After external force ceases, damaged dynamical microtubules effectively self-repair as tubulin monomers from the background suspension incorporate back into the damaged regions.
source: Furthermore, after the external force ceases the damaged filaments effectively self-repair, as the tubulin monomers from the background suspensions incorporate back into the damaged regions.
evidence: Referring to findings from Schaedel et al., 2015

claim: Stabilized microtubule filaments do not show any aging phenomena.
source: In comparison, here we study stabilized filaments that do not show any aging phenomena.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The regions of high strain might be the location where monomers preferentially dissociate from dynamical microtubule filaments.
source: However, it seems plausible that the ovalization and the formation of kinks is also relevant to dynamical microtubules, and the regions of high strain might be the location where monomers preferentially dissociate from filament.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis connecting ovalization to monomer dissociation

claim: The softening of microtubules is analogous to phenomena observed in carbon nanotubes.
source: It is also worth noting that the softening of microtubules we observe is analogous to phenomena that have already been observed and quantified in carbon nanotubes (e.g. see reviews by [Thostenson et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2007]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thostenson et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2007

claim: Experiments on carbon nanotubes demonstrate the formation of a single kink, followed by a multiple kink pattern upon further bending.
source: In particular, experiments demonstrate the formation of a single kink, followed by a multiple kink pattern upon further bending (Iijima et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Iijima et al., 1996

claim: Simulations of carbon nanotubes predict a reduction in effective nanotube stiffness, as the buckling force drops and remains almost constant after kinking.
source: while simulations predict a reduction in effective nanotube stiffness, as the buckling force drops and remains almost constant after kinking eYakobson1996.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yakobson 1996

claim: Hysteresis due to plastic deformations triggered by kinking events has been observed in multi-walled carbon nanotubes.
source: Hysteresis due to plastic deformations triggered by kinking events has also been observed, at least in the case of multi-walled carbon nanotubes (Jensen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2007

claim: Micron-long microtubules subject to buckling forces of a few pN become more mechanically compliant at relatively low strains due to significant cross-sectional deformations and subsequent buckling.
source: In conclusion, we have found that micron-long microtubules subject to buckling forces of a few pN become more mechanically compliant at relatively low strains due to significant cross-sectional deformations and subsequent buckling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and simulation results

claim: The critical curvatures for the softening transition are surpassed in the beating of Chlamydomonas flagella.
source: This result seems biologically relevant, as the critical curvatures for the softening transition are surpassed, for instance, in the beating of Chlamydomonas flagella.
evidence: Based on comparison of critical curvatures with literature values for flagellar curvatures

claim: The softening of microtubules with increasing strain provides an explanation for the discrepancy between values of flexural rigidity inferred by passive versus active methods.
source: Additionally, the softening of MTs with increasing strain provides an explanation for the discrepancy between values of flexural rigidity inferred by passive (thermal fluctuations) versus active methods, since the latter typically access higher strains and thus infer effectively lower rigidities.
evidence: Based on the finding that microtubules soften at high strains

claim: The mechanical properties of microtubules can be quantitatively summarized by three elastic moduli, even for very large strains.
source: Despite the complex nature of microtubules, we found that their mechanical properties - at least as concerning buckling experiments via optical trapping - can be quantitatively summarized by three elastic moduli, even for very large strains, and need to be accounted for to explain observations that arise naturally in many biological systems.
evidence: Supported by successful fitting of experimental data with 3D model using three elastic moduli

claim: Tubulin was purified from bovine brain tissue according to an established protocol.
source: Tubulin was purified from bovine brain tissue according to the established protocol (Castoldi and Popov, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castoldi and Popov, 2003

claim: Filaments subjected to repeated cycles of compression/extension do not seem to exhibit any aging.
source: Filaments subjected to repeated cycles of compression/extension do not seem to exhibit any aging (Figure 2B, inset).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B inset

claim: The position of the detection bead is sampled with the QPD at a rate of 100 KHz and averaged in bins of 1000 samples.
source: The position of the detection bead is sampled with the QPD at a rate of 100 KHz and averaged in bins of 1000 samples, effectively resulting in a sampling rate of 100 Hz, that is about 100 times per step.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: Presence of biotin either throughout the filaments or in localized segments does not affect the measured single filament buckling force.
source: Presence of biotin either throughout the filaments or in localized segments does not affect the measured single filament buckling force.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The experiments seem consistent with an essentially rigid microtubule-bead attachment.
source: In the end, our experiments seem consistent with an essentially rigid microtubule-bead attachment.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of a flat region near zero strain in force-strain curves
